Despise
dē-spīz´
v. (to esteem as worthless; to look down upon; rendering Hebrew bazah, Greek kataphroneo, exoutheneo)
From Latin despicio, to look down upon. The word is a verdict of the eye: to despise a thing is to appraise it and price it at nothing, which is why Scripture uses it of how men valued the Messiah.

Biblical Definition

To despise is to reckon a thing worthless, and Scripture's gravest use of the word describes the world's valuation of Christ: “He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief: and we hid as it were our faces from him; he was despised, and we esteemed him not” (Isaiah 53:3). The prophet does not say He was hated, which would at least concede importance; He was not esteemed, priced at nothing, passed over. The same verb measures what God will not do with a broken man: “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise” (Psalm 51:17). What men throw away, God receives. Turned toward instruction, despising marks the fool by definition: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge: but fools despise wisdom and instruction” (Proverbs 1:7). Folly here is not ignorance but appraisal — the fool has weighed wisdom and found it not worth having. Paul applies the word to the most dangerous form of contempt, which wears the face of comfort: “Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering; not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance?” (Romans 2:4). Patience unrepented of is patience despised.

Webster 1828 Definition

To contemn; to scorn; to disdain; to have the lowest opinion of. Scripture uses it of men despising the Messiah, of God refusing to despise a contrite heart, of fools despising wisdom, and of sinners despising the goodness that leads to repentance.

expand to see more

DESPISE, v.t. [L. despicio; de and specio, to look.] To contemn; to scorn; to disdain; to have the lowest opinion of.

2. To abhor; to slight; to neglect as unworthy of regard.

3. To undervalue; to esteem lightly; as, to despise riches or honors.

DESPISED, pp. Contemned; scorned; disdained; neglected.

DESPISER, n. A contemner; a scorner; one who slights or undervalues.

DESPICABLE, a. That may be or deserves to be despised; contemptible; mean; vile; worthless.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 53:3 — "He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief: and we hid as it were our faces from him; he was despised, and we esteemed him not."

Psalm 51:17 — "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise."

Proverbs 1:7 — "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge: but fools despise wisdom and instruction."

Romans 2:4 — "Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering; not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance?"

Modern Corruption

Contempt has been redistributed: it is thought shameful to despise anything the age approves, and unremarkable to despise the wisdom, the reproof, and the forbearance that Scripture says only a fool prices at nothing.

expand to see more

The age is sensitive to contempt directed at persons and blind to contempt directed at truth. To despise a man is rightly held to be wrong; to despise instruction, correction, and the accumulated wisdom of the fathers is treated as independence of mind. Proverbs 1:7 divides the two plainly. The fool is not defined by low intelligence but by his appraisal — he has looked at wisdom and priced it at nothing. That contempt is invisible to the man holding it, because it feels like discernment; and it is unteachable, because instruction is the very thing being despised.

The subtlest despising is the one Romans 2:4 names, and almost nobody recognizes it as contempt at all. God's goodness, forbearance, and longsuffering delay a judgment that is deserved; and the man who takes the delay as evidence that nothing is owed has not merely misread the delay but insulted it. Presumption is contempt wearing the face of comfort. Isaiah 53:3 shows where such appraisal finally lands: it was not rage that met the Messiah but the settled verdict that He was not worth esteeming. Recover the true scale, and a man will fear despising the patience of God more than he fears the scorn of men.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew bazah (to despise, to hold in contempt) governs Isaiah 53:3 and Psalm 51:17; Greek kataphroneo (to think down upon) and exoutheneo (to count as nothing) carry the New Testament sense.

expand to see more

Hebrew bazah (H959) — to despise, disdain, hold in contempt; the verb of the despised Servant in Isaiah 53:3.

Hebrew ma'ac (H3988) — to reject, refuse, spurn; the companion word for casting a thing away as worthless.

Greek kataphroneo (G2706) — to think down upon, to despise; the verb of Romans 2:4 for despising God's goodness.

Greek exoutheneo (G1848) — to make of no account, to set at nought; used of despising a brother and of the base things God chose.

Hebrew muwcar (H4148) — instruction, correction, discipline; the thing fools despise in Proverbs 1:7.

Usage

"“He was despised, and we esteemed him not” — the verdict was not hatred but a price of nothing."

"“A broken and a contrite heart… thou wilt not despise” — what men discard God receives."

"“Despisest thou the riches of his goodness” — presumption is contempt for divine patience."
